kurz: Which three variables determine the debt-to-GDP ratio, how states have historically reduced their debt and who bore the cost in each case.

bloecke.md:
Absolute levels of debt say very little. The usual approach is to relate them to annual economic output. The [[debt-to-GDP ratio]] is the stock of debt divided by nominal gross domestic product. Methodologically this is a makeshift solution, because a stock is divided by an annual flow. The ratio is useful nonetheless, because it makes countries and decades comparable.

Two conclusions follow from this. First, the ratio falls even without any repayment, as long as the denominator grows faster than the numerator. Second, inflation benefits the debtor. It raises nominal GDP and at the same time erodes the value of existing debt fixed in euros.

bloecke.unter: Ratios below the 60% reference value set in the EU Treaty have long been the exception.

bloecke.md: The 122.6% for the US covers only federal debt. The 88.9% for the euro area refers to general government as defined under Maastricht, that is central, state and local government and social security combined. The two figures therefore do not measure the same thing. A comparison without this caveat creates a gap that does not exist in that form. In addition, these are gross debt figures. Government assets such as equity holdings, receivables and reserves are not netted against them.

## Three drivers of the debt-to-GDP ratio

The debt-to-GDP ratio changes according to a fairly simple relationship. The state pays interest on the existing stock of debt and alongside this records a [[primary balance]], that is the difference between revenue and expenditure excluding interest payments. In addition, economic output grows in nominal terms. The primary balance is fought over in parliament. The interest burden, by contrast, stems from past debt, and growth cannot be decreed.

bloecke.erklaerung: The change in the debt-to-GDP ratio in percentage points per year. What matters is the gap between the interest rate and nominal growth, and not the level of the interest rate.

bloecke.beispiel: b = 64%, r = 3%, g = 2%, primary balance of zero: Δb = 0.64 × 0.01 / 1.02 = +0.63 percentage points a year.

bloecke.md: The decisive term is `r − g`. If nominal growth is above the average interest rate, the ratio falls even if the state permanently runs a small primary deficit. If the sign reverses, the ratio rises even with a balanced primary budget, and the higher it already is, the faster it rises. This is why high levels of debt can become unstable without any change in policy.

bloecke.md:
The table shows an asymmetry. In a favourable interest rate environment, a country with a ratio of 120% can afford a primary deficit of just over 1% of GDP without the ratio rising. If the interest rate is two percentage points above growth, the same country needs a primary surplus of 2.3%, a budget swing of around 3.5 percentage points, just to hold the ratio steady. Such adjustments can rarely be sustained politically.

The inertia of the average interest rate works in the debtor's favour. It only rises when old bonds mature and are replaced at higher cost. The yield on ten-year German federal bonds (Bunds) averaged −0.51% in 2020, 2.61% in 2025, 3.18% in August 2026 and around 3.5% in mid-September 2026. This turnaround only has its full effect on the budget over the course of a decade. Because this happens slowly, it is easily ignored, but over time it can use up all room for manoeuvre.

## The state's creditors

Government debt is matched by the assets of the creditors. The creditors are banks, insurers, pension institutions, investment funds, foreign investors and central banks. In late summer 2026 the Eurosystem still held around €1,667 billion of government bonds from the PSPP purchase programme. Since July 2023 maturing securities have no longer been replaced, and the holdings are shrinking by roughly €15-34 billion a month. The bonds are thus passing back to private buyers, who demand a yield for taking them on.

The statement “we owe it to ourselves” is correct in accounting terms and still misleading in economic terms. It ignores the fact that taxpayers and bondholders are not the same people. Reducing debt through taxes burdens taxpayers; reducing it through inflation or default burdens creditors. The composition of the creditors therefore determines who bears the costs. A high foreign share also shifts this distributional question across national borders.

## The debt brake (Schuldenbremse)

Since 2009, Articles 109 and 115 of the Basic Law (Grundgesetz) have limited new borrowing. The federal government may take on new structural borrowing of at most 0.35% of GDP, and the federal states none at all until 2025. In addition, there is a cyclical component that allows more borrowing in a downturn, and an emergency clause for natural disasters and exceptional emergencies. The emergency clause requires a repayment plan and was used in the pandemic years.

In March 2025 the rule was considerably relaxed. Since then, defence spending above 1% of GDP no longer counts against the debt brake, and the federal states were given their own leeway of 0.35%. In addition, a debt-financed special fund (Sondervermögen) of €500 billion for infrastructure, with a term of twelve years, was added. The German ratio has been rising again since then, from 63.0% in the third quarter of 2025 to 64.4% in the first quarter of 2026.

bloecke.md:
## Five ways out of a high level of debt

Historically there are only five ways, and they can be combined: growing (g rises), saving (primary surplus), inflating (the numerator stays the same in nominal terms while the denominator rises with inflation), **financial repression** (the real interest rate is pushed artificially below growth) and defaulting (suspension of payments or debt restructuring). Only the first way burdens nobody, and it is the only one that no government can decide on directly.

[[Financial repression]] is the least conspicuous way. It includes interest rate caps, capital controls, regulatory incentives for banks and insurers to hold government bonds, and a central bank that keeps interest rates low. It leads to a negative real interest rate. Creditors get their money back in full in nominal terms, but considerably less in real terms. Carmen Reinhart and M. Belen Sbrancia have shown that after 1945 the industrialised countries reduced their war debts mainly in this way, without repaying them.

bloecke.md: Roughly adding up the annual values from 2012 to 2023 gives investors who held ten-year Bunds a real loss of around 18 percentage points. The debtor gained by the same order of magnitude. Summing annual values is only a rough calculation, but it shows the direction. The state is relieved of debt in real terms even if it does not repay a single cent. An investment that is safe in nominal terms can therefore produce losses in real terms.

In October 2009 Greece revised its budget deficit from 3.7% to 12.7% of GDP. The debt-to-GDP ratio had risen from 104.6% (2007) to 128.5% (2009). There followed rescue packages of €110 billion (2010), €164.4 billion (2012-2014) and €86 billion (2015-2018, of which €61.9 billion was disbursed).

The debt restructuring followed in March 2012. Private creditors gave up 53.5% of the face value, and through maturity extensions and coupon cuts they lost around 75% of the present value. The costs for the country itself were just as high. Real GDP shrank by around 26% between 2008 and 2013, and unemployment reached about 26% in 2014.

A state without its own central bank cannot reduce its debt through inflation; it is left with saving or default. A government bond is therefore not risk-free even within a monetary union.

On 20 November 1923 one US dollar cost 4.2 trillion marks; in July 1914 it had been 4.20 marks. As a result, the Reich's domestic war debts lost their value, as did every savings balance and every fixed-interest bond in private hands. The conversion into the Rentenmark took place at a rate of one Rentenmark to one trillion paper marks.

The currency reform of 20/21 June 1948 repeated this pattern in a controlled form. Wages, rents and pensions were converted at 1:1, savings balances initially at 10:1. Out of 100 Reichsmark, around 6.50 Deutsche Mark ultimately remained. In both cases the state was relieved of its debt at the expense of the holders of monetary assets, while real assets and debtors were spared.

## MMT and the standard criticism

Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) starts from an accurate observation. A state with its own fiat currency cannot be forced into nominal insolvency in that currency, because it can always pay. According to MMT, it is therefore only inflation that sets a real limit on government spending.

This is where the standard criticism comes in. First, nobody knows this inflation limit in advance; it only becomes apparent once it has been exceeded. Second, because of budget procedures and election dates, fiscal policy reacts much more slowly than a central bank. In practice, tax rises as a brake on inflation can hardly be pushed through. Third, monetary financing of the state jeopardises the independence of the central bank, and in the euro area it is prohibited anyway under Article 123 TFEU (Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union). Fourth, the core claim does not apply to any euro member, because none of them has its own currency. Greece in 2012 is the empirical proof of this.

Complacency shows in the statement “The state cannot go bankrupt.” In nominal terms this is true for countries with their own currency. For creditors, however, it is no consolation, because repression and inflation inflict real losses on them just as a debt haircut does, only more slowly and without public attention.

Scaremongering shows in the statement “The debt-to-GDP ratio is rising, so state bankruptcy is coming.” A ratio of 64% or 90% says nothing about sustainability on its own. What matters are r − g, the maturity structure, the currency of the debt and whether the country's own central bank stands behind it. For decades Japan has carried a ratio that by any rule of thumb should have led to collapse long ago, but in its own currency and with domestic creditors.

Five figures are enough for an initial assessment: the debt-to-GDP ratio, the primary balance, the difference between the average interest rate and nominal growth, the average remaining maturity of the debt and the currency in which it is denominated. A long remaining maturity delays the effect of rising interest rates. Debt in foreign currency belongs in a different risk class.

mitnehmen: The debt-to-GDP ratio depends on the primary balance, the average interest rate and nominal growth, and the gap between the interest rate and growth determines whether it falls or rises of its own accord.

The higher the ratio, the larger the budget swing that a turn in the interest rate cycle forces; at 120% and an r − g of +2 points, a primary surplus of 2.3% of GDP is needed just to hold the ratio steady.
Debt can be reduced through growth, saving, inflation, financial repression or default; three of the five ways come at the expense of creditors, two of them without public attention.
Nominal repayment does not protect against real losses; from 2016 to 2023 the real interest rate on ten-year Bunds was negative every year.
A state with its own currency cannot become insolvent in nominal terms, but a euro member can; the Greek debt restructuring of 2012 cost private creditors around three quarters of the present value.

begriffe.text: A state's stock of debt divided by its nominal annual GDP. The ratio can fall without any repayment if the economy grows faster than the stock of debt.

The difference between government revenue and government expenditure excluding interest payments. Unlike the interest burden from past debt, the primary balance can be steered directly by policymakers.
The gap between the average nominal interest rate on the stock of debt and nominal GDP growth (r − g). If it is negative, the debt-to-GDP ratio falls of its own accord with a balanced primary budget.

Reduction of government debt through an interest rate kept artificially below inflation, supported by regulation and capital controls. The creditor is paid in full in nominal terms, but only partly in real terms.
